blocks.heading: Choosing a participation arrangement
blocks.text: A quality circle is a small group meeting to identify and suggest solutions to work or quality problems. A worker council provides a representative forum for wider workplace matters. Democratic leadership consults workers and considers their views when making decisions. They differ in purpose, membership and scope. Choose a quality circle for a specific recurring technical problem when the workers have useful knowledge and time to investigate. A representative council can suit changes affecting many departments, while direct democratic discussion can suit a manageable team. Participation takes time and needs relevant information. It should not delay an urgent safety response or create a false promise that every suggestion must be accepted.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tano Print has a recurring sealing defect on one line. Operators know the process and can investigate it during scheduled problem-solving time. A quality circle suits the focused defect better than creating a broad council solely for that issue. Management should evaluate and respond to proposals. For an organisation-wide change to shifts, a representative council would provide broader coverage.

blocks.heading: Quality circles
blocks.text: A quality circle is a small group of workers meeting regularly to identify, investigate and suggest solutions to work or quality problems. It draws on practical knowledge and can support recognition and satisfaction. Members need relevant information, time and a management response. It is not automatically a decision-making board or a forum for every employment issue. A proposal still needs assessment against cost, safety and other constraints.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Rena Packaging’s line operators examine why seals fail and propose a change after reviewing the pattern. Their focused practical investigation fits a quality circle. Management should evaluate the proposal and explain its response instead of leaving the group with no feedback.

blocks.heading: Worker councils
blocks.text: A worker council is a representative forum through which workers’ views on wider workplace matters can be discussed with management. Representation helps include different groups when consulting everyone directly is impractical. Clear selection, scope, information and reporting back matter to credibility. It differs from a small quality circle focused on a specific work problem. Consultation does not by itself mean workers own the business or have a veto over every decision.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Onda Stores has several departments affected by new opening hours and seeks representatives from each to discuss the change. A council can gather varied concerns and communicate proposals across departments. Representatives must report back so participation does not end with the few people at the table.

blocks.heading: Democratic leadership
blocks.text: Democratic leadership involves consulting employees, encouraging contributions and considering their views in decisions. It can use practical knowledge and build acceptance, especially where staff have relevant experience. It can take time and requires an explanation of who makes the final decision. It is not a promise that every view prevails or that consultation suits an immediate emergency before action.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Ema Repairs’ manager asks the experienced team to compare two workable appointment systems before choosing. The discussion can reveal practical problems and build understanding. The manager should explain the final choice, including why some suggestions were not adopted.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain which participation method fits each issue: Hela Print’s small operator group studies recurring ink faults, while representatives from all departments discuss a proposed common shift policy.

The focused operator problem-solving group is a quality circle. The cross-department representative forum fits a worker council. Both involve workers but differ in purpose and membership; choosing one requires identifying whether the issue is a specific work problem or a wider representative concern.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Participation, conflict and representation
blocks.text:
Nara Packaging plans a new shift arrangement across production, sales and dispatch. Workers feel excluded and believe the allocation is unfair. Management can allow two weeks for discussion and is comparing a worker council with a small quality circle originally formed to study sealing defects.

a Explain how unclear participation and perceived unfairness could cause conflict at Nara, and how an appropriate forum could help. [8]
b Evaluate whether the benefits of participation outweigh its costs before Nara’s shift change. [12]

a Exclusion can make workers believe management ignores practical needs, while an unexplained allocation encourages suspicion of unfairness. This can weaken cooperation and obstruct the change. Representatives from each affected department can gather concrete concerns, compare the staffing constraints and report responses back. Participation must precede the final decision and include a credible response; a forum used only to announce it may deepen distrust. b Worker input can reveal scheduling conflicts, improve fairness and support acceptance. Consultation takes time and representatives can disagree, but two weeks are available and the issue affects the whole operation. Use a representative council with a clear timetable, decision scope and feedback process. The benefit outweighs the manageable delay because the present conflict concerns exclusion and fairness. Management should explain any rejected proposal rather than promise that every demand will be accepted; urgent action without time for discussion would require a different balance.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Participation, conflict and representation
blocks.text:
Nara Packaging plans a new shift arrangement across production, sales and dispatch. Workers feel excluded and believe the allocation is unfair. Management can allow two weeks for discussion and is comparing a worker council with a small quality circle originally formed to study sealing defects.

a(i) Define worker participation. [2]
a(ii) State one advantage and one disadvantage of participation. [2]
b State two possible causes of organisational conflict. [2]
c Explain how meaningful participation could help Nara’s dispute. [6]
d Evaluate a representative council compared with using the existing quality circle for the shift decision. [8]

a(i) Employees contribute to decision-making in the business. a(ii) Their knowledge can improve decisions; consultation can take time. b Perceived unfairness and poor communication. c Staff can explain how shifts affect different tasks and raise the perceived unfairness before the policy is final. Management can explain constraints and respond to evidence, potentially improving both the rota and acceptance. Simply announcing the final arrangement would not provide the same influence. d The shift change affects several departments, so a representative council fits the breadth and can gather different concerns. The quality circle has relevant problem-solving experience but its original membership and defect focus do not ensure fair cross-department representation. Choose the council with clear scope and feedback to staff; retain the circle for its focused quality task.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Participation, conflict and representation
blocks.text:
Tuli Print has a recurring machine-quality problem confined to one line. Operators understand it and management has time to investigate. It compares a quality circle with a representative council covering all departments. For part (b) only, the decision now concerns a common shift policy affecting every department rather than the single-line quality problem. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate the two participation arrangements for Tuli’s original problem. [12]
b Evaluate the choice after the issue becomes the common shift policy. Explain whether the judgement changes. [12]

a A quality circle fits the operators’ knowledge and narrow quality problem. It can improve decisions and satisfaction through genuine influence, though proposals need feasibility checks. A broad council adds representation that the specific task does not currently require. Choose the circle and respond to its findings; participation should solve the issue rather than exist as a label. b A common shift policy affects employees beyond one line, so the circle no longer provides sufficient representative coverage. Use a worker council with views from each affected department, clear information and reporting back. It may take longer, but consultation can address perceived fairness and reduce conflict before implementation. The recommendation changes because the scope of the decision changes; the circle remains useful for focused technical work.
